:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x) = 2\sqrt{x} -4x$ at the point $(1,-2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}-4x) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}-4x) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2}-4.\end{aligned}
$$

     

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1) = (1)^{-1/2} - 4 = -3,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m' = -\dfrac{1}{m} = \dfrac 1 3.
$$

The equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(-2) & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y+2 & =\frac{1}{3}(x-1) \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{1}{3}-2 \\ y & =\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}x-\frac{7}{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{3}x & =\frac{7}{3} \\ x & =7.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(7,0).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2{x}^{2}+x$ at the point $(1,3)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x)=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{2}+x)=4x+1.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=4(1)+1=5,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-3 & =-\frac{1}{5}(x-1) \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{1}{5}+3 \\ y & =-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{5}x+\frac{16}{5} & =0 \\ x & =16.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(16,0).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $y$-axis.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{′}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt{x}) \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2{x}^{1/2}) \\  & ={x}^{-1/2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{′}(1)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1}}=1,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{′}=-\frac{1}{m}=-1.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-1(x-1) \\ y & =-x+1+2 \\ y & =-x+3.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $y$-axis by setting $x=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =-0+3 \\ y & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $y$-axis at  $(0,3).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=2\sqrt[4]{x}$ at the point $(1,2)$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at
$($
{{field-1}}$,$
{{field-2}} $).$
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}^{'}(x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(2\sqrt[4]{x}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{1/4}) \\  & =2\cdot \frac{1}{4}{x}^{-3/4} \\  & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{x}^{3}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m={f}^{'}(1)=\frac{1}{2\sqrt[4]{{1}^{3}}}=\frac{1}{2},
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
{m}^{'}=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)}=-2.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-2 & =-2\cdot (x-1) \\ y & =-2x+2+2 \\ y & =-2x+4.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}-2x+4 & =0 \\ 2x & =4 \\ x & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(\,2,0\,).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $f(x)=10 x^{2} + 5 x$ at the point $(1,15)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}f'(x)=\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}x}(10 x^{2} + 5 x)=20 x + 5.\end{aligned}
$$

So the slope of the tangent line is

$$
m=f'(1)=25=25,
$$

and therefore the slope of the normal line is

$$
m'=-\frac{1}{m}=-\frac{1}{(25)}=- \frac{1}{25}.
$$

Finally, the equation of the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}y-(15)&=- \frac{1}{25}(x-(1))\\y&=- \frac{1}{25}x-\left(- \frac{1}{25}\right)+(15)\\y&=- \frac{1}{25}x+\frac{376}{25}.\end{aligned}
$$

Lastly, we find the point of intersection with the $x$-axis by setting $y=0$ and solving the resulting equation. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}- \frac{1}{25}x+\frac{376}{25}&=0\\x&=376.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(376,0).$

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Let $f(x)=2\sqrt{x}-3x+1$. Find where the normal line to the curve $y=f(x)$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $4$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $x$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First find the point on the curve:

$$
f(4)=2\sqrt{4}-3(4)+1=4-12+1=-7.
$$

Thus the normal passes through $(4,-7)$. Differentiate both variable terms:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=2x^{1/2}-3x+1,\\
f'(x)&=x^{-1/2}-3=\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}-3.
\end{aligned}
$$

The tangent slope is

$$
f'(4)=\frac{1}{2}-3=-\frac{5}{2}.
$$

The normal slope is the negative reciprocal, so

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{-5/2}=\frac{2}{5}.
$$

Using $(4,-7)$, the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
y+7&=\frac{2}{5}(x-4),\\
y&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{8}{5}-7\\
&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{43}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Solving gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=\frac{2}{5}x-\frac{43}{5},\\
2x&=43,\\
x&=\frac{43}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $\left(\frac{43}{2},0\right)$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem: Find where the normal line to the curve $y=x^2$ at the point $(1,1)$ intersects the $x$-axis.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Differentiating gives

$$
f'(x)=2x,\qquad f'(1)=2.
$$

The tangent slope is $2$, so the normal slope is its negative reciprocal:

$$
m_n=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

The diagram shows the curve, its solid tangent, and its dashed normal at $(1,1)$.

![The parabola y equals x squared with its tangent and perpendicular normal at (1,1).](images/31/31ba09ff14e5bd485794f283c5d6a5b087b6c21fdb9242af01b75ec8e8744e0d.png)

Using point-slope form, the normal line is

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-1&=-\frac{1}{2}(x-1)\\
y&=-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{2}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$. Therefore,

$$
0=-\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{3}{2},\qquad x=3.
$$

The intersection is $(3,0)$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=3\sqrt{x}$ at the point $(4,6)$ intersects the $y$-axis.

The normal line intersects the $y$-axis at $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
Rewrite the radical as a fractional power and differentiate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=3x^{1/2},\\
f'(x)&=\frac{3}{2}x^{-1/2}=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At $(4,6)$, the tangent slope and normal slope are

$$
f'(4)=\frac{3}{2\sqrt{4}}=\frac{3}{4},\qquad m_n=-\frac{1}{3/4}=-\frac{4}{3}.
$$

The normal passes through $(4,6)$, so

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-6&=-\frac{4}{3}(x-4),\\
y&=-\frac{4}{3}x+\frac{16}{3}+6\\
&=-\frac{4}{3}x+\frac{34}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $y$-axis, $x=0$, giving $y=\frac{34}{3}$. The intersection is $\left(0,\frac{34}{3}\right)$.

First find the point on the curve.

$$
f(4)=-4\sqrt{(4)}-3(4)=-20.
$$

The normal passes through $(4,-20)$.

Rewrite the radical or reciprocal using powers, then differentiate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=- 4 x^{\frac{1}{2}} - 3 x, \\f'(x)&=-3 - \frac{2}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=-3 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}.

Evaluate the tangent slope and take its negative reciprocal to find the normal slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_t=f'(4)&=-3 - \frac{2}{\sqrt{(4)}}=-4, \\m_n=-\frac{1}{m_t}&=-\frac{1}{(-4)}=\frac{1}{4}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use point-slope form through $(4,-20)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-(-20)&=\frac{1}{4}(x-(4)), \\y&=\frac{x}{4} - 21.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $y$-axis, $x=0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&=\frac{1}{4}\cdot 0+(-21), \\y&=-21.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $(0,-21)$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=4\sqrt{x}+x-1$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $1$ intersects the $x$-axis.

The intersection is $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First find the point on the curve.

$$
f(1)=4\sqrt{(1)}+(1)-1=4.
$$

The normal passes through $(1,4)$.

Rewrite the radical or reciprocal using powers, then differentiate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=4 x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x - 1, \\f'(x)&=1 + \frac{2}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=1 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope and take its negative reciprocal to find the normal slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_t=f'(1)&=1 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{(1)}}=3, \\m_n=-\frac{1}{m_t}&=-\frac{1}{(3)}=- \frac{1}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use point-slope form through $(1,4)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-(4)&=- \frac{1}{3}(x-(1)), \\y&=- \frac{x}{3} + \frac{13}{3}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $x$-axis, $y=0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
0&=- \frac{1}{3}x+\left(\frac{13}{3}\right), \\x&=13.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $(13,0)$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
Find where the normal line to the curve $y=4\sqrt{x}+3x+2$ at the point with $x$-coordinate $1$ intersects the $y$-axis.

The intersection is $(${{field-1}}$,$ {{field-2}}$)$. Give exact values.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
First find the point on the curve.

$$
f(1)=4\sqrt{(1)}+3(1)+2=9.
$$

The normal passes through $(1,9)$.

Rewrite the radical or reciprocal using powers, then differentiate.

$$
\begin{aligned}
f(x)&=4 x^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3 x + 2, \\f'(x)&=3 + \frac{2}{x^{\frac{1}{2}}}=3 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{x}}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the tangent slope and take its negative reciprocal to find the normal slope.

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_t=f'(1)&=3 + \frac{2}{\sqrt{(1)}}=5, \\m_n=-\frac{1}{m_t}&=-\frac{1}{(5)}=- \frac{1}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

Use point-slope form through $(1,9)$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y-(9)&=- \frac{1}{5}(x-(1)), \\y&=- \frac{x}{5} + \frac{46}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

At the $y$-axis, $x=0$.

$$
\begin{aligned}
y&=- \frac{1}{5}\cdot 0+\left(\frac{46}{5}\right), \\y&=\frac{46}{5}.
\end{aligned}
$$

The intersection is $\left(0,\frac{46}{5}\right)$.
